paragraphs: An agent that has learned several skills should ideally be able to combine them when a new task arrives. This paper gives that idea a precise logical structure: tasks form a Boolean algebra, so new objectives can be expressed using AND, OR, and NOT applied to previously learned base tasks.

The method learns goal-oriented value functions and then combines those functions according to specific rules. These functions provide the information needed to choose actions for the composed objectives. Under restrictions on the tasks' transition dynamics, the authors prove that these combinations recover optimal policies for every task expressible in the algebra, without additional learning.

The approach is tested in two domains, including a high-dimensional video game that requires function approximation. After learning base skills, the agent composes them to address a super-exponential number of new tasks. The significance is that logical task descriptions become a mechanism for reusing learned behavior. The optimality result depends on the stated transition restrictions; it is not a claim about unrestricted combinations of arbitrary skills.
neurips-2020-a-boolean-task-algebra-for-.tldr: Under restrictions on task dynamics, Boolean combinations of learned value functions yield optimal policies for new tasks without further learning.

paragraphs: Many decisions require first predicting unknown quantities and then solving an optimization problem using those predictions. Training the predictor through the optimization problem can improve the resulting decisions, but it requires repeatedly solving and differentiating through a potentially expensive computation. Non-smooth behavior can also prevent this training process from improving decision quality.

This paper learns a smaller surrogate for the optimization problem alongside the predictor. It represents the feasible space using meta-variables, each formed as a linear combination of the original variables. Training both components together makes the compact representation responsive to the decisions the system needs to make, rather than treating dimensionality reduction as a separate preliminary step.

The authors report reduced training and inference time together with better performance. They attribute these benefits to concentrating on important optimization variables and learning in a smoother space. Experiments demonstrate improvements in non-convex adversary modeling, submodular recommendation, and convex portfolio optimization. These findings support learning the optimization representation itself as a way to make decision-focused prediction both more efficient and more effective.
neurips-2020-automatically-learning-comp.tldr: Jointly learning a compact optimization surrogate and a predictor improves decision quality while reducing computation in the reported tasks.

paragraphs: Knowledge base completion predicts missing facts from facts already recorded. Embedding methods do this by representing knowledge geometrically, but their representations can restrict which facts or logical relationships they can express. The paper targets several such restrictions together, including hierarchies, relations involving more than two entities, and the incorporation of logical rules.

BoxE represents entities as points and relations as collections of multidimensional boxes. These spatial structures encode basic logical properties while supporting a fully expressive model. The same design naturally handles higher-arity relations, extending its scope beyond knowledge graphs built only from pairwise relationships.

The model can both capture rules and accept supplied rules from rich classes of rule languages. This matters because learned representations can use logical information beyond isolated inference patterns. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on benchmark knowledge graphs and more general knowledge bases, along with empirical benefits from integrating rules. The contribution combines representational capability with evidence that its geometric treatment of logic helps predict missing facts.
neurips-2020-boxe-a-box-embedding-model-.tldr: BoxE represents entities as points and relations as boxes to combine expressive knowledge completion with higher-arity relations and logical rules.

paragraphs: SAT solvers search for an assignment satisfying a Boolean formula or establish that no such assignment exists. Their branching choices influence the work required. Graph-Q-SAT learns these choices using value-based reinforcement learning and a graph neural network, with the aim of making better early decisions when conventional heuristics are still warming up.

The learned heuristic examines each problem's structure and is trained through interaction with MiniSat. It preserves solver completeness: the resulting solver still produces a satisfying assignment or a proof of unsatisfiability. The authors report data-efficient training without elaborate dataset preparation or feature engineering, and reductions of two to three times in the iterations needed to solve problems.

The reported generalization includes unsatisfiable instances, problems with five times as many variables as training examples, and positive transfer to a different task family without additional training. On larger problems, fewer iterations also reduce elapsed solving time. The authors nevertheless frame this as a proof of concept, with further work needed to reduce wall-clock time in modern SAT solving settings.
neurips-2020-can-q-learning-with-graph-n.tldr: Graph-Q-SAT learns branching decisions that reduce SAT search iterations and show transfer while preserving solver completeness.

paragraphs: Reconstructing causal structure becomes difficult when hidden variables influence multiple observed quantities and experiments do not reveal which variables they changed. This paper studies that combination, using observational data together with soft interventions whose targets are unknown. Its goal is to characterize and learn the causal structures compatible with these sources of evidence.

The authors introduce a property called psi-Markov that connects the observed distributions to both a causal graph and a set of intervention targets. It uses relationships that remain invariant across observational and experimental conditions, going beyond conditional independences alone. They then give a graphical test for whether two graph-and-target descriptions belong to the same equivalence class.

An accompanying algorithm learns that equivalence class from the combined data. The authors prove soundness and completeness in the sample limit: the method identifies every edge endpoint that can be oriented within the class. This is a maximal-information guarantee relative to the defined equivalence class, rather than a promise that every underlying causal graph or intervention target becomes uniquely identifiable.
neurips-2020-causal-discovery-from-soft-.tldr: The paper characterizes and learns causal equivalence classes from observational data and soft interventions with unknown targets, allowing shared latent causes.

paragraphs: In multi-label classification, a single input can receive several labels. Hierarchical multi-label classification adds a further requirement: the predicted labels must respect a hierarchy connecting the classes. This makes prediction a joint problem, because the relationships among labels constrain which outputs are coherent.

The paper introduces C-HMCNN(h), an approach built around a network h for the underlying multi-label problem. It uses the hierarchy information to produce predictions consistent with the required constraint while also seeking better classification performance. The central contribution is therefore a way to bring known class relationships into the predictions of a multi-label network.

The authors report an extensive experimental comparison in which C-HMCNN(h) performs better than state-of-the-art models. That finding supports using the hierarchy as useful predictive information as well as a requirement on valid outputs. The approach addresses two linked needs: predicting the appropriate labels and ensuring those predictions fit the structure of the classification task. Its reported advantage concerns the evaluated hierarchical classification problems.
neurips-2020-coherent-hierarchical-multi.tldr: C-HMCNN(h) uses class hierarchies to produce coherent multi-label predictions and improves performance in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: One explanation of visual illusions is that perception reflects how likely particular image patches are in the visual world. On this view, the statistical regularities of ordinary images help explain why some arrangements produce misleading impressions of lightness or color. The paper develops a computational way to investigate that explanation.

The authors introduce a tool that learns from a large image dataset and estimates the likelihood of image patches. They use it to construct a model that accounts for both lightness and color illusions within one framework. Treating both kinds of illusion through the same statistical tool connects them to a shared explanatory principle.

The tool can also be applied in reverse to generate visual illusions in natural images. This extends its role from explaining existing effects to producing images that exhibit them. Together, the explanatory model and the generation capability support the input-driven account described in the paper. The findings provide computational support for that approach, rather than establishing it as the only possible explanation of visual perception.
neurips-2020-color-visual-illusions-a-st.tldr: A model of image-patch likelihoods provides a unified statistical explanation of lightness and color illusions and can generate new illusions.

paragraphs: Understanding stochastic gradient descent requires explaining how learning evolves, not just where it ends. This paper studies that evolution for a single-layer neural network classifying a high-dimensional Gaussian mixture with two possible labels. The setting provides a model of a non-convex loss landscape that includes interpolating regimes and a large generalization gap.

The authors define a stochastic process that gives SGD a continuous-time extension, called stochastic gradient flow. In the full-batch limit, this construction recovers standard gradient flow. They then use dynamical mean-field theory from statistical physics to describe learning through a self-consistent stochastic process in the high-dimensional limit.

This produces a closed-form analysis of the learning dynamics in the specified model. By varying control parameters, the authors explore algorithm performance and how optimization moves through the loss landscape. The value of the framework is an analytically tractable view of stochastic learning behavior. Its conclusions concern the stated Gaussian-mixture classification setting and high-dimensional analysis, rather than arbitrary neural-network training problems.
neurips-2020-dynamical-mean-field-theory.tldr: Dynamical mean-field theory gives a closed-form description of SGD learning dynamics for a single-layer Gaussian-mixture classifier in high dimensions.

paragraphs: In contextual bandits, a policy chooses actions based on the current context. Off-policy evaluation asks how well a policy would perform using data gathered under a different policy. This paper addresses both estimating that value and expressing uncertainty about the estimate, so that existing data can also guide the search for better policies.

The authors apply empirical likelihood to construct a policy-value estimator and a confidence interval. Both are formulated as simple convex optimization problems. They then use the interval's lower endpoint as the objective for policy optimization, searching for policies with high reward lower bounds. This makes uncertainty part of the selection criterion instead of relying only on a point estimate.

Empirically, the estimator and confidence interval improve over earlier proposals when data are finite. The resulting policy-learning algorithm also outperforms a strong off-policy learning baseline. The contribution ties evaluation and optimization together: the same uncertainty-aware framework both assesses a candidate policy and supplies the quantity used to search for promising alternatives.
neurips-2020-empirical-likelihood-for-co.tldr: Empirical likelihood supports policy-value estimation, confidence intervals, and policy learning that maximizes a reward lower bound from off-policy data.

paragraphs: Online multiclass classification requires making successive predictions while learning from feedback. This paper introduces Gaptron, a randomized first-order algorithm, and analyzes its mistakes through surrogate losses: training objectives that stand in for the discrete error of predicting the wrong class. The analysis makes direct use of the gap between those quantities.

With full information, the authors give expected mistake bounds relative to logistic, hinge, and smooth hinge losses, with regret of order K for K classes. Under bandit feedback, they establish expected regret of order K times the square root of T, where T is the number of rounds. The expectations are over the algorithm's own randomness.

The paper identifies Gaptron as the first linear-time algorithm achieving that bandit regret rate. Its expected mistake bound also avoids dependence on feature-vector dimension, unlike earlier algorithms with the same stated regret order. The proof technique is a separate contribution: exploiting the surrogate gap provides a route to strong bounds without relying on the exp-concavity or mixability properties traditionally used for such analyses.
neurips-2020-exploiting-the-surrogate-ga.tldr: Gaptron exploits the gap between classification error and surrogate losses to obtain strong expected regret bounds with efficient online updates.

paragraphs: Federated learning commonly coordinates agents through gradient-based training, but some collaborative tasks provide no useful gradients. Hyperparameter tuning is one example of expensive black-box optimization. This paper extends Bayesian optimization to such federated settings, allowing agents to collaborate on optimization tasks through a method called federated Thompson sampling.

The method approximates the Gaussian process surrogate using random Fourier features. This representation supplies parameters that agents can exchange. Building the algorithm around Thompson sampling substantially reduces how many parameters must be communicated, connecting the optimization strategy directly to the practical cost of collaboration.

The authors provide a convergence guarantee that is robust to heterogeneity among agents, addressing the challenge that participating agents need not be identical. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness in communication efficiency, computational efficiency, and practical performance. The contribution broadens federated collaboration to expensive function evaluations without gradients, while giving both a communication-conscious construction and theoretical support for convergence with heterogeneous participants.
neurips-2020-federated-bayesian-optimiza.tldr: Federated Thompson sampling enables collaborative black-box optimization with reduced parameter exchange and a convergence guarantee robust to heterogeneous agents.

paragraphs: Useful representations should expose low-dimensional structure while preserving distinctions between classes. This paper proposes maximal coding rate reduction, or MCR², as an information-theoretic objective for that purpose. It maximizes the difference between the coding rate of the full dataset and the combined coding rates of the individual classes.

The comparison encourages representations that retain diversity across the dataset while making class-specific structure compact. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for diverse, discriminative features and relate the objective to cross-entropy, information bottleneck, information gain, and contractive and contrastive learning. They also show that coding rates can be accurately computed from finite samples for degenerate distributions with subspace-like structure.

The principle supports supervised, self-supervised, and unsupervised representation learning within one framework. In the reported classification experiments, using this objective alone produces substantially greater robustness to corrupted labels than cross-entropy. The authors also report that self-learned invariant features can yield state-of-the-art clustering of mixed data. These findings support coding-rate reduction as a representation objective with benefits extending beyond standard classification accuracy.
neurips-2020-learning-diverse-and-discri.tldr: MCR² learns diverse, class-discriminative representations through coding-rate differences, with reported benefits for label-corruption robustness and clustering.

paragraphs: Ranking data can contain several distinct patterns of preference or performance. Models centered on one total ordering can struggle to represent that richness, while explicitly combining multiple models can make learning difficult. This paper introduces contextual repeated selection, or CRS, to represent multimodal ranking distributions through advances in choice modeling.

The approach brings contextual choice structure into a model of rankings, providing a natural way to capture multiple modes. The authors analyze maximum likelihood estimation and derive structure-dependent bounds on both expected risk and tail risk. These results address estimation quality as well as the model's ability to express richer distributions.

The analysis also yields tight expected-risk bounds for the multinomial logit choice model and the Plackett-Luce ranking model, plus a tail-risk bound for Plackett-Luce, which the authors identify as first results of their kinds. Empirically, CRS significantly outperforms existing methods across real-world ranking settings, including racing and ranked-choice voting. The contribution combines a more flexible ranking model with theoretical guarantees about learning it from data.
neurips-2020-learning-rich-rankings-0fad.tldr: Contextual repeated selection captures multimodal ranking patterns and combines strong empirical performance with risk guarantees for maximum likelihood estimation.

paragraphs: Machine learning systems often make discrete decisions such as sorting items, selecting neighbors, or finding shortest paths. These operations can be straightforward to compute but interrupt back-propagation, preventing earlier components from learning through the decision procedure. This paper develops a systematic way to turn optimizers into differentiable operations.

The method introduces stochastic perturbations into optimization. The resulting operations are differentiable and never locally constant, so the construction avoids regions where the operation remains unchanged throughout a neighborhood. It works with existing solvers, permits efficient derivative evaluation, and uses the noise amplitude to control smoothness. These properties make discrete optimization more accessible within end-to-end learning pipelines.

The authors also connect the framework to a family of structured-prediction losses and establish theoretical guarantees for their use in learning. Experiments demonstrate the approach across several tasks. The contribution is a general bridge between optimization procedures and gradient-based training, allowing the solver's decisions to participate in learning rather than functioning only as a final computational step.
neurips-2020-learning-with-differentiabl.tldr: Stochastic perturbations turn optimization procedures into differentiable operations that can be used with existing solvers in end-to-end learning.

paragraphs: Pauses in speech contain useful information for removing background noise. During an interval without speech, the recording exposes noise on its own. This paper builds a deep learning denoising model around those incidental pauses, using only a single audio channel to learn about the interference mixed with the speaker's voice.

The model detects silent intervals across time and uses them to learn noise dynamics. This matters because the noise can change during a recording: multiple pauses reveal its evolving features, rather than just providing one fixed noise example. The learned information is then used to suppress noise in the speech signal.

Experiments on multiple datasets support the importance of detecting these intervals. The method outperforms several state-of-the-art denoisers in the reported comparisons, including systems using audio alone and systems using both audio and visual information. It also generalizes to spoken languages absent from training. These results support treating naturally occurring speech pauses as informative observations that can improve denoising from a single-channel recording.
neurips-2020-listening-to-sounds-of-sile.tldr: A speech denoiser learns changing background noise from pauses in single-channel audio and shows strong performance and cross-language generalization.

paragraphs: An agent navigating a realistic environment sees only part of its surroundings at a time, making memory important for longer tasks. MultiON tests that memory by requiring navigation to a sequence of objects specified for each episode. It extends single-object navigation and explicitly asks agents to find goal objects they have previously observed.

The benchmark lets the authors compare agent models as navigation tasks become more complex. Its focus is the role of map-like memory: remembering what was seen and where it was located should help when a later goal refers to an earlier observation. The experiments compare several ways of representing that information.

Performance drops sharply as complexity increases. A simple semantic-map agent performs surprisingly well relative to more complex agents whose maps contain neural image features. Even agents with oracle maps achieve relatively low performance. Together, these findings show that richer map representations do not automatically produce better navigation, and that effectively using map information remains a substantial challenge in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2020-multion-benchmarking-semant.tldr: MultiON tests memory through sequential object navigation and finds that increasing complexity challenges even agents equipped with oracle maps.

paragraphs: A complexity measure is useful when it helps predict how a trained network will perform beyond its training examples. Designing such measures for deep networks has proved difficult. This paper proposes Neural Complexity, or NC, which learns a measure from experience across tasks instead of specifying the measure entirely by hand.

NC is a meta-learning framework: interactions with many heterogeneous tasks train a model to produce a single scalar complexity value for predicting generalization. That value also has a practical training role. Once learned, the NC model can contribute an additional regularization term to the ordinary supervised training loss of a task learner.

The authors compare this approach with manually designed complexity measures and other meta-learning models, and validate it on multiple regression and classification tasks. The contribution links two uses of complexity: assessing generalization and influencing training through regularization. Learning the measure across varied tasks provides a data-driven way to pursue both goals within a shared framework.
neurips-2020-neural-complexity-measures-.tldr: Neural Complexity learns a scalar measure across tasks to predict generalization and regularize supervised learning.

paragraphs: Neural population recordings can be summarized as low-dimensional trajectories, but smooth temporal patterns do not by themselves identify underlying dynamics. Standard Gaussian process priors cannot distinguish dynamics from other temporal correlations. This paper introduces trajectory priors that express temporal non-reversibility: movement with a directional structure that cannot simply occur backward.

The authors encode this property in multi-output Gaussian process covariance functions. These can replace standard kernels in multivariate regression and latent-variable models. Their GPFADS model uses the kernels to represent single-trial population activity through low-dimensional latent processes with dynamical structure. A Kronecker factorization makes learning and inference fast and memory-efficient.

On synthetic data, GPFADS recovers the true phase portraits, capturing how latent states move through their space. It also provides a probabilistic generalization of jPCA, a method for detecting rotational neural dynamics. Applied to monkey motor-cortex recordings, it discovers strongly rotational latent trajectories. The contribution adds directional dynamical structure to a probabilistic modeling framework that supports uncertainty quantification and principled model selection.
neurips-2020-non-reversible-gaussian-pro.tldr: GPFADS uses non-reversible Gaussian process priors to identify directional latent dynamics, including rotations, in neural population activity.

paragraphs: In online linear optimization, a learner repeatedly chooses an action before encountering its cost. This paper studies a setting where K hint vectors arrive before each decision. The challenge is to benefit from several sources of advice when their usefulness may emerge through a combination, rather than through a single hint considered alone.

The authors develop an algorithm with logarithmic regret whenever some convex combination of the hints positively correlates with the cost vectors. A convex combination blends the hints using nonnegative weights that sum to one. The guarantee is conditional on the existence of this useful blend, extending earlier work restricted to one hint.

To obtain the result, the paper introduces a broader method for combining arbitrary online linear optimization algorithms. The combined learner's regret is within a logarithmic factor of the smallest regret achieved by those algorithms in hindsight. This gives the work a second contribution beyond advice vectors: a general way to assemble online algorithms while retaining performance close to the best constituent.
neurips-2020-online-linear-optimization-.tldr: An online optimization algorithm achieves logarithmic regret when a convex combination of available hints positively correlates with costs.

paragraphs: Randomized sketching reduces the dimensionality of computations used in optimization. This paper studies iterative Hessian sketch methods for least-squares problems, asking how the choice of random projection affects convergence. It focuses on subsampled randomized Hadamard transforms and truncated Haar matrices, using random matrix theory to compare them with greater precision.

The analysis extends results about the limiting spectrum of projected matrices and derives a new formula for the second moment of their inverses. These mathematical tools yield simple expressions for asymptotically optimal step sizes and convergence rates. They connect the statistical structure of the projection to concrete choices made by the iterative algorithm.

The resulting rates are identical for Haar and randomized Hadamard projections, and asymptotically better than those for Gaussian projections. The asymptotic qualification matters: the result describes the limiting analysis rather than asserting the same ordering for every finite problem. The authors also suggest that these techniques may support analysis of other algorithms using randomized dimensionality reduction.
neurips-2020-optimal-iterative-sketching.tldr: Random matrix analysis yields asymptotically optimal sketching steps and shows matching Haar and Hadamard convergence rates that improve on Gaussian projections.

paragraphs: Training data may come from people or agents who want particular predictions for themselves. Such contributors differ both from independent random samples and from adversaries whose sole goal is to undermine learning. This paper studies that middle ground through a Stackelberg competition model for least-squares regression.

The model explicitly represents data providers as self-interested agents seeking desired predictions. Accounting for that strategic behavior produces a non-convex optimization problem. The authors derive an algorithm with global convergence, improving on approaches whose guarantees stop at local optima. The guarantee concerns the optimization problem arising from this particular model of agent incentives.

Experiments use the medical personal costs and red wine datasets. The authors report improvements over algorithms optimal under adversarial assumptions and over the state of the art in the reported comparisons. These results support matching the learning formulation to contributors' actual objectives: modeling targeted self-interest can lead to a different and more effective solution than treating every strategic data provider as purely malicious.
neurips-2020-optimal-learning-from-verif.tldr: A strategic regression model accounts for self-interested data providers and admits a globally convergent algorithm with reported empirical improvements.

paragraphs: Simplicity bias is the tendency of training procedures such as SGD to favor simple models. It has been used to explain good generalization, but that explanation must also accommodate neural networks' fragility. This paper constructs piecewise-linear and image-based datasets with explicitly defined simplicity and several predictive features of different complexity.

Through theory and experiments, the authors find that this preference can become extreme: networks may rely exclusively on the simplest feature while ignoring more complex predictive features. They argue that this behavior could explain sensitivity to seemingly mild distribution changes and small adversarial perturbations. The proposed explanation is a possible link between feature preference and non-robustness.

The same bias can also harm generalization within the original data distribution, because the simplest feature may be less predictive than alternatives. Ensembles and adversarial training can fail to remove the problem in the studied settings. The datasets and methods therefore provide a testbed for examining when simplicity helps, when it becomes restrictive, and whether new training approaches can avoid these failures.
neurips-2020-the-pitfalls-of-simplicity-.tldr: Theory and experiments show that extreme preference for simple features can harm both robustness and ordinary generalization.

paragraphs: Data useful for a prediction task can also reveal sensitive attributes that contributors would prefer to conceal. This paper develops a theoretical framework for attribute obfuscation, examining how a learned representation can remain useful while reducing an adversary's ability to infer a designated attribute.

The authors formulate the problem as minimax optimization and analyze inference guarantees against worst-case adversaries within their framework. They also establish an information-theoretic lower bound describing the fundamental tension between task accuracy and information leakage. This makes the trade-off an object of analysis, rather than treating usefulness and concealment as goals that can always be improved independently.

Experiments on two real-world datasets corroborate the inference guarantees and the inherent trade-offs. Among the alternatives evaluated, adversarial learning achieves the best balance between hiding the attribute and preserving accuracy. The result supports this approach in the reported comparisons while grounding its purpose in a theoretical account of what information must be retained or exposed to maintain predictive performance.
neurips-2020-trade-offs-and-guarantees-o.tldr: A minimax framework provides attribute-inference guarantees and characterizes the trade-off between concealing sensitive information and maintaining prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: Top-down decision-tree methods choose successive splits using criteria such as information gain or Gini impurity. This paper identifies a restriction of these criteria: they consider correlations between the target and individual attributes. The proposed extension also examines correlations involving small groups of attributes, allowing interactions to influence split selection.

For Boolean inputs and Boolean targets under the uniform distribution, the authors prove a guarantee that applies to every target function. Given a reference tree size s and an error tolerance, the algorithm constructs a potentially much larger tree whose error is bounded by a constant multiple of the best size-s tree's error plus that tolerance. The construction has an explicit size bound that grows with s and tighter tolerance.

The analysis uses noise stability, a measure of a function's smoothness. The result circumvents impossibility findings for existing splitting heuristics, which can fail even on simple targets. Its strength is broad coverage of target functions within the stated distributional setting; the comparison does not promise to match the reference tree's size.
neurips-2020-universal-guarantees-for-de.tldr: A decision-tree splitting criterion using small attribute groups provides approximation guarantees for all Boolean targets under the uniform distribution.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference is appealing for large neural networks but difficult to perform efficiently. Variational inference offers scalable approximations, yet its objective can over-regularize over-parameterized models. This paper addresses that problem by changing how the approximation is represented, drawing inspiration from structured random-matrix methods developed for kernels.

Walsh-Hadamard Variational Inference, or WHVI, uses Walsh-Hadamard-based factorizations to reduce the number of parameters and accelerate computation. The structured representation is intended to avoid the over-regularization issues of the variational objective. Its design links the size and computational organization of the approximation to the behavior of Bayesian learning.

The authors provide extensive theoretical and empirical analyses, reporting substantial speedups and model reductions compared with other approximate-inference techniques for over-parameterized models. The contribution therefore concerns both the cost of inference and the suitability of its parameterization. More broadly, it demonstrates a concrete route by which advances in kernel methods can improve approximate Bayesian inference for deep and convolutional neural networks.
neurips-2020-walsh-hadamard-variational-.tldr: WHVI uses structured Walsh-Hadamard factorizations to reduce Bayesian neural-network inference costs and address variational over-regularization.
